beats.act: why a whole document loses precision
beats.narration_text: Embed a forty-page benefits manual as one vector, and that vector carries everything at once — vacation, health coverage, retirement, parental leave, travel. A question about vacation days can only match it approximately, because the same vector is also encoding everything that has nothing to do with vacation. Pack more topics into one chunk and you are averaging them.

shot.visual_intent: the whole-document collapse: five topic bands in one manual converge into a single averaged point

all five bands converge inward and collapse into ONE dot

caption settles: one vector, averaged across every topic

props.headline: One Document, One Vector
props.caption: One vector has to represent every topic at once — so the signal for any one of them is an average across all of them.
props.sparkLine: Everything at once, so nothing sharply.

beats.act: the size tradeoff runs both ways
beats.narration_text: So cut it smaller. But this tradeoff runs in both directions. Too small, and a chunk loses the context that gave it meaning — "five days per year" is useless if you cannot tell five days of what. Too large, and you have rebuilt the whole-document problem in miniature. There is no correct number to look up.

shot.visual_intent: a size axis with a failure mode at each end — chunks shrinking to a context-less fragment on the left, growing to a diluted block on the right

right end: chunks grow into one fat block, its one fact diluted among the rest
the middle stays deliberately unmarked — no number is offered
caption settles: the right size depends on the document

props.headline: Too Small. Too Large.

props.middleNote: no universally correct setting — it depends on the structure and density of the document
props.caption: Practitioner guidance suggests testing a range rather than assuming one size fits every use case (Pinecone, “Chunking Strategies for LLM Applications”).

beats.role_note: FALSIFIABILITY — the chapter explicitly refuses to settle this one; the reel must not settle it either.
beats.narration_text: Should neighbouring chunks share a little text at the seam? The rationale is clean — a fact that straddles a boundary survives in one piece instead of being cut in half. Common practice says yes, a modest overlap. But a 2026 controlled study found no measurable benefit to answer quality, and higher indexing cost. Hold this one loosely.

beats.narration_text: Here is the chapter's own figure, redrawn. Cut at a fixed character count and you slice straight through a sentence, mid-word. Cut at paragraph and heading boundaries, and the text stays intact. Or use embeddings to detect where the meaning actually shifts, and split there. Same page, three cuts — only two of them respect what is written.

beats.act: how the tooling actually does it
beats.narration_text: How the tooling actually does it: try a prioritized list of separators. Paragraph breaks first. Then line breaks. Then individual spaces. Drop to a smaller unit only when the larger one would produce an oversized chunk — so paragraphs stay whole whenever they possibly can. LangChain's recursive splitter is one example of the pattern. The pattern is the point, not the library.

shot.visual_intent: the separator ladder — three rungs tried in priority order, each falling back only when the chunk would be oversized

rung 2 lights: line breaks
rung 3 lights: individual spaces — the last resort
the rule settles under the ladder, then the 'illustrative, not an endorsement' note

beats.narration_text: Predict before I show you. One forty-page benefits manual. One question: how many vacation days do I get in my second year? Now chunk that manual three ways — as one whole document, by fixed character count, or at paragraph and heading boundaries. Which one puts the complete answer inside a single chunk?

beats.role_note: WORKED EXAMPLE — the chapter's own, run against its own question.
beats.narration_text: Whole document: the question matches one vector carrying the entire manual — you retrieve everything, or you cannot tell this manual from the next one. Fixed count: the vacation table splits mid-row, and the sentence naming the policy lands in a different chunk from the number it refers to. Structure-aware: the vacation section stays whole, second-year increase included.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap. A whole document embedded as one vector averages every topic it contains, so no single question matches it sharply. Chunk size fails in both directions — too small loses context, too large loses precision. Overlap is a guard with a clear rationale and an unsettled payoff. And splitting at the document's own boundaries beats splitting at arbitrary counts. Chunking is a design decision, and chapter five asks the next one: how do you search thousands of these chunks fast?

artifactLines: A whole document as one vector averages every topic in it — a specific question can only match it approximately.
Chunk size fails in BOTH directions: too small loses the context that gave a fact meaning, too large dilutes it. No universal number.
Overlap guards a fact that straddles a boundary — but a 2026 controlled study found no measurable benefit and higher indexing cost. Unsettled.
Splitting at the document's own boundaries — paragraphs, headings, meaning shifts — beats splitting at arbitrary counts.
Next (Ch. 5): hundreds or thousands of chunks. How do you search them fast?

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — the prompt is read aloud verbatim, then discussed.
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this: "Here is a document I actually work with. I'll describe its structure. Propose a chunking strategy — approximate size, whether to use overlap, and where the boundaries should fall. Then argue the opposite case as strongly as you can, and tell me which failure would cost me more: a chunk too small to carry its context, or one too large to match precisely." That second half is the part that matters. Anything will hand you a confident first answer; making it argue against itself is how you find out whether the recommendation was reasoned or reflexive. Bring a document whose structure you already know, and see whether its boundaries match the ones you would have drawn.
